0.note: The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

1.note: Here David is speaking as if Yahweh were actually a physical place of safety or shelter. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I trust in you, Yahweh, to keep me safe] or [I depend on you, Yahweh, to protect me]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please do not ever let me have shame; please deliver me in your righteousness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because you are righteous]

2.q: הַטֵּ֤ה אֵלַ֨⁠י ׀ אָזְנְ⁠ךָ֮ מְהֵרָ֪ה הַצִּ֫ילֵ֥⁠נִי הֱיֵ֤ה לִ֨⁠י ׀ לְֽ⁠צוּר־מָ֭עוֹז
2.note: David is using imperative forms, but these communicate a polite request rather than commands. If the imperative form does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use forms in your language that communicate polite requests. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please incline your ear to me; please rescue me quickly; please be for me a rocky summit of refuge]

Here David is using the term **ear** to mean hearing or attention. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Listen and respond to me] or [Pay attention to me]

Here David is speaking as if Yahweh were actually a **rocky summit** used as a **refuge** and as if he were actually a place that had **strongholds** where he could hide and be safe from his enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [be for me like a rocky summit of refuge, and like a dwelling place of strongholds]

David is using these possessive forms, **a rocky summit of refuge** and **a dwelling place of strongholds**, to describe places that are characterized by providing refuge and strength. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive forms for this, you could express these ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [be for me a rocky summit that provides refuge, a stronghold in which to dwell]

3.note: Here David is speaking as if Yahweh were actually a large **rock** and a **stronghold** to which he could flee to be safe from his enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [you are like a rock that I can flee to for safety and like a stronghold in which I can be safe]
David is using the term **name** to refer to God’s reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language as in the UST.

The terms **lead** and **guide** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [direct me]

Here the Hebrew verbs that the ULT translates as **you lead me and guide me** could be: (1) expressing a general truth that has been part of David’s ongoing experience. If you decide this is the meaning, then you can translate the two verbs in this phrase in a similar way to the ULT. (2) expressing something that will happen in the future. Alternate translation: [you will lead me and guide me] or (3) a request that is a prayer to Yahweh. (This option is less likely since David does not use the imperative forms of these verbs as would be expected if these verbs were meant to be requests.) Alternate translation: [lead me and guide me] or [please lead me and guide me]

The implication is that David wants God to lead and guide him so that his enemies do not harm him. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [you lead me and guide me so that my enemies do not harm me]

4.note: Here David is speaking as if his enemies’ plans to harm him were a **net** that they had hidden to trap him. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Rescue me from being harmed by the plans that they have secretly made to harm me] or [Rescue me from the ambush that they have secretly set for me]

Here the Hebrew verb that the ULT translates as **You will pull me** could be: (1) expressing something that will happen in the future as in the ULT or (2) a request that is a prayer to Yahweh. (This option is less likely since David does not use the imperative form of this verb as would be expected if this was a request.) Alternate translation: [Please pull me] or [Pull me]

Here David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a **refuge**, a physical place of safety and protection from danger. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you are my protector] or [you keep me safe]

5.note: Here, **hand** represents God’s power, control and care. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Into your care] or [Into your control]

David is using the term **spirit** to mean his enlivening spirit that causes him to be physically alive. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I commit myself]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [God who is faithful to me]

6.note: Here, **the ones keeping** represents those who worship idols. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I hate those who worship]

David is using the possessive form to describe **idols** that are characterized by **worthlessness**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [worthless idols]

7.note: The terms **be glad** and **rejoice** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [I will rejoice greatly]

7.q: בְּ⁠חַ֫סְדֶּ֥⁠ךָ אֲשֶׁ֣ר רָ֭אִיתָ אֶת־עָנְיִ֑⁠י יָ֝דַ֗עְתָּ בְּ⁠צָר֥וֹת נַפְשִֽׁ⁠י
7.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **covenant faithfulness** and **affliction**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [because you are faithful to your covenant, for you have seen how I have suffered; you have known how my soul is troubled]

David is using the term **soul** to mean the entire person from the perspective of his spiritual and emotional existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the troubles I have experienced] or [my inner distress]

8.note: Here, **hand** represents the power or control of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [into the power of the ones being hostile to me] or [under the control of the ones being hostile to me]

Here David is speaking of being rescued as if he had been squeezed into a narrow, dangerous space with no way to escape and God enabled him to escape into an **open space**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you have set me free from danger] or [you have rescued me from my desperate situation]

9.note: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please be gracious to me]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **grief**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for I am distressed, because of my grieving my eye has wasted away]

David says **my eye has wasted away from grief** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [I cry so much that my eyes feel like they are wasting away] or [I am crying so much that my eyes hurt]

Here, **grief** represents crying. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from crying] or [because I cry so much]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [my soul and my body have wasted away from grief]

David is referring to all of himself by naming two major components, **my soul** and **my body**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all of me] or [my whole being]

10.q: כִּ֤י כָל֪וּ בְ⁠יָג֡וֹן חַיַּ⁠י֮ וּ⁠שְׁנוֹתַ֪⁠י בַּ⁠אֲנָ֫חָ֥ה כָּשַׁ֣ל בַּ⁠עֲוֺנִ֣⁠י כֹחִ֑⁠י וַ⁠עֲצָמַ֥⁠י עָשֵֽׁשׁוּ
10.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [For my life comes to an end with sorrow, yes, my years with groaning; my strength fails from my iniquity, indeed, my bones waste away]

By **For my life has come to an end with sorrow**, David means that his life is being consumed or shortened by grief and distress. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [For my life is being consumed by sorrow] or [For sorrow is shortening my life]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **sorrow**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [sorrowfully]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because I have sinned] or [because of the wrong things I have done]

David is using one part of his body, his **bones**, to represent his entire physical being as it deteriorates. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and my entire body wastes away]

11.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **reproach**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [I have become someone whom people reproach] or [I have become someone whom people despise]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and I have become especially a reproach to my neighbors, and I have become a dread to the ones knowing me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **dread**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the ones knowing me are afraid of me]

12.note: The expression **I have been forgotten** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [People have forgotten me]

David is making a comparison between himself and **a dead man out of mind**. The point of this comparison is that just as a dead man is completely forgotten by people, so David feels that he has been completely forgotten. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [I have been completely forgotten, just as people forget about the dead]

David is using **out of mind** as a common expression of the culture to mean “completely forgotten.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [is completely forgotten] or [whom people have completely forgotten]

Here David is comparing himself to **a broken vessel** using the word **like**. The point of this comparison is that just as a broken vessel is useless and discarded, so David feels useless and discarded by others. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [I am useless like a broken vessel] or [I am discarded like a broken vessel]

13.q: כִּ֤י שָׁמַ֨עְתִּי ׀ דִּבַּ֥ת רַבִּים֮ מָג֪וֹר מִ⁠סָּ֫בִ֥יב
13.note: David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [For I hear the whispering of many, and there is terror on every side]

13.q: כִּ֤י שָׁמַ֨עְתִּי ׀ דִּבַּ֥ת רַבִּים֮ מָג֪וֹר מִ⁠סָּ֫בִ֥יב
13.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **terror on every side** with the information about **the whispering of many**. Alternate translation: [For I hear the whispering of many and there is terror on every side]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **terror**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [terrifying things on every side]

David is using **they plan to take my life** as a common expression of the culture to mean “they plan to kill me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they plan to murder me]

14.note: David uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between his distressing circumstances and his trust in Yahweh. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [However, I] or [Yet I]

David is not using this possessive form **my God** to indicate that he possesses or controls Yahweh. Rather he is using these words to indicate that Yahweh is the God whom he worships. If it would help your readers, you could indicate this explicitly as in the UST.

15.note: Here, **hand** represents the power or control of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [My times are in your control; rescue me from the power of]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please rescue me]

David assumes that readers will know that **My times** refers to the events and circumstances of his life, including its duration. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [The events of my life] or [My life and circumstances]

The terms **the ones being hostile to me** and **the ones pursuing me** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [my relentless enemies]

16.note: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please make your face shine upon your servant; save me]

David is using **Make your face shine on** as a common expression of the culture to mean “show favor to” or “be gracious to.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Show favor to] or [Be gracious to]

David is speaking of himself in the third person as **your servant** to show humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a humble form in the first person. Alternate translation: [me, your servant]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because you are faithful to your covenant]

17.note: By using **let**, the psalmist is expressing what he thinks should happen. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [the wicked should have shame; they should be silent in Sheol]

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because I have called upon you, Yahweh, do not let me have shame]

David is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are wicked]

David assumes that readers will know that **Sheol** is the place of the dead. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [let them be silent in the place of the dead]

18.note: The expression **Let lying lips be silenced** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [May God silence lying lips] or [May lying lips become silent]

Here, **lying lips** represents people who tell lies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those who lie]

David is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase as in the UST.

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **pride** and **contempt**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [proudly and contemptuously] or [in a proud and contemptuous manner]

The terms **pride** and **contempt** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [with great arrogance]

19.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **goodness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [How incredibly good you are] or [How abundant are the good things you do]

David is speaking of God’s goodness as if it were something physical that God had **stored up** like treasure in a storehouse. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express the meaning plainly as in the UST.
See how you translated the similar phrase “I take refuge” in 31:1.

The psalmist is using **sons of man** as a common expression of his culture to mean “human beings.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all people]

20.q: תַּסְתִּירֵ֤⁠ם ׀ בְּ⁠סֵ֥תֶר פָּנֶי⁠ךָ֮ מֵֽ⁠רֻכְסֵ֫י אִ֥ישׁ תִּצְפְּנֵ֥⁠ם בְּ⁠סֻכָּ֗ה מֵ⁠רִ֥יב לְשֹׁנֽוֹת
20.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [You hide them in the safety of your presence, protecting them from those who plot against them and from cruel words]

Here David is speaking of **the hiding-place of your presence** as if it were a physical shelter where Yahweh could hide people from danger. David means that Yahweh protects people by his divine presence and power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You protect them by your presence from the plots of man]

David is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language as in the UST.

Here David is speaking of God’s protection and help as if it were a physical **shelter** in which God would hide righteous people from the accusatory words of evil people. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [you protect them from people who attack with their words as if you were hiding them in a shelter]

Here, **tongues** represents people speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from people who accuse them with their words] or [from verbal attacks]

21.note: The expression **Blessed be** is a passive verbal form. The psalmist is expressing his desire to praise Yahweh. If it would be unnatural to use that form for this purpose, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I bless Yahweh] or [Let me praise Yahweh]

21.q: בָּר֥וּךְ יְהוָ֑ה כִּ֥י הִפְלִ֘יא חַסְדּ֥⁠וֹ לִ֝֗⁠י בְּ⁠עִ֣יר מָצֽוֹר
21.note: David is giving the reason that Yahweh should be blessed after stating that he should be blessed. If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because he has shown marvelously his covenant faithfulness to me in a besieged city, blessed be Yahweh]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [all the ways he is faithful to his covenant]

The expression **in a besieged city** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is his enemies. Alternate translation: [in a city that my enemies had surrounded]

22.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **alarm**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when I was alarmed]

Here, **eyes** represents God’s attention or awareness. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I am cut off from your attention] or [you are no longer watching over me]

David uses the words **But indeed** here to indicate a contrast between his fearful thoughts and God’s actual response. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [However] or [Yet]
Here, **voice** represents the pleas themselves. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language as in the UST.

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [when I cried out to you, you heard the voice of my pleas]

23.note: David is using the adjective **faithful** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [faithful people] or [those who are faithful]

24.note: David is using **Be firm** as a common expression of the culture to mean “be strong.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly as in the UST.
The word **your** is plural here because David is speaking to **all the ones waiting for Yahweh**. Use the plural form in your language if your language marks that distinction.
Here the **heart** represents where a person’s thoughts and feelings exist. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly as in the UST.

David assumes that readers will know that here **waiting** refers to waiting on Yahweh to help them. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [all the ones waiting for Yahweh to help you]
